title: Tuckman's stages of team development
blurb: Name Tuckman's five stages in order, recognise each from team behaviour and know what the leader does at each.
question: Three weeks into a project, a team that started out polite and quiet is now arguing about who does what and how the work should be done. Which Tuckman stage has it reached, and how should the project manager lead it?

teach.body: Bruce Tuckman's model describes how a group of individuals becomes an effective team. His original 1965 model had four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. A fifth, adjourning, was added in 1977 for when the team breaks up. A project manager uses the model to recognise which stage the team is in, adapt their leadership style to it, anticipate storming rather than be surprised by it, and plan team-building.

steps.label: Forming
steps.sub: Polite, unsure, dependent on the leader

steps.label: Norming
steps.sub: Agreed ways of working, cohesion grows

teach.caption: Memory hook: the endings rhyme. Form, storm, norm, perform, then adjourn.

teach.h: What the leader does at each stage
teach.caption: Adjourning: the leader recognises achievement, captures lessons learned and helps people move on.

items.label: adjourning added as the fifth stage

teach.body: Sam leads a bridge refurbishment team. In week one people are polite and keep asking Sam what to do (forming), so Sam sets clear goals and roles. By week four the structural and traffic engineers are arguing about methods (storming): Sam coaches them through it and clarifies who decides what. By month three they have agreed ways of working (norming) and Sam facilitates. By month five they run their own work (performing) and Sam delegates. At handover Sam thanks everyone and captures lessons (adjourning).

Progress is not one-way. A significant change, such as a new member joining, a key person leaving, a new leader or a change in goals, can send a team back to an earlier stage, often storming or even forming. The leader recognises the slip and switches back to the matching style: more direction or coaching, and some renewed team-building, until the team settles again.

teach.text: Storming is a NORMAL stage, not a sign of a bad team. Don't pick options that suppress or ignore the conflict, or that delegate fully during storming. Also watch the leader-style match: DIRECT when forming, COACH when storming, SUPPORT when norming, DELEGATE when performing.

items: Order: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning (fifth stage added 1977).
Leader style: direct, coach, support, delegate; then recognise and close at adjourning.
Use the model to recognise the stage, adapt style, anticipate storming and plan team-building.
Big changes can send a team back to an earlier stage.

summary: You can now name Tuckman's five stages in order, recognise each from how the team behaves, and match the leader's style to it: direct, coach, support, delegate, then recognise and close. You can also explain how a project manager uses the model and why a change can send a team back a stage.

A.q: What is the correct order of the first four stages in Tuckman's model?
A.why: The order is forming, storming, norming, performing; adjourning follows as the fifth stage.

whyNot.0: Norming comes after storming: teams agree ways of working once conflict is resolved.
whyNot.1: Forming is always first: the group must come together before it can storm.
whyNot.3: Norming comes before performing: agreed ways of working underpin high performance.

A.q: A newly assembled project team is polite and cautious, and keeps asking the project manager what to do. Which Tuckman stage is this?
A.why: Polite, unsure behaviour and dependence on the leader are the signs of forming.

whyNot.1: Storming involves open conflict and challenge, not polite caution.
whyNot.2: Norming involves agreed ways of working and growing cohesion.
whyNot.3: Adjourning is when the task is complete and the team disbands.

A.q: During the storming stage, what should the project manager mainly do?
A.why: Storming needs a coaching leader who manages conflict and clarifies roles and approach.

whyNot.0: Full delegation suits performing; during storming the team still needs active help.
whyNot.2: Storming is normal; disbanding the team is not the answer.
whyNot.3: Celebrating and capturing lessons belongs to adjourning.

B.q: Which stage was added to Tuckman's model in 1977?
B.why: Adjourning was added in 1977 to cover the team breaking up once the task is complete.

whyNot.0: Norming was one of the original four stages from 1965.
whyNot.1: Storming was one of the original four stages from 1965.
whyNot.2: Transforming is not a stage in Tuckman's model.

B.q: Team members have accepted their roles, agreed how they will work together and cohesion is growing. Which stage is this, and what leader style fits?
B.why: Agreed ways of working and growing cohesion mean norming, where the leader supports and facilitates.

whyNot.0: Storming is marked by conflict, which this team has moved past.
whyNot.2: Forming teams are still unsure and dependent on the leader.
whyNot.3: Adjourning is when the work is complete and the team disbands.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a way a project manager uses Tuckman's model?
options: Adapting leadership style to the stage
Anticipating storming and planning for it
Choosing roles to balance the team
B.why: Choosing roles to balance a team is what Belbin's team roles are used for, not Tuckman's stages.

whyNot.0: Recognising the stage is the first use of Tuckman's model.
whyNot.1: Adapting style to the stage is a key use of the model.
whyNot.2: Anticipating storming and planning team-building is a key use of the model.

C.q: Halfway through a project, the team leader changes and two new engineers join. Arguments about methods break out in a team that had been working smoothly. What has happened, and what should the PM do?
options: Reverted to storming; coach and resolve
Reached performing; now delegate even more
Now norming; leave it to settle itself
C.why: Big changes in membership and leadership can send a team back to storming. The PM coaches, manages the conflict and renews team-building.

whyNot.1: Arguments about methods are not a sign of performing; delegating more would leave the conflict unmanaged.
whyNot.2: The project is not finished, so the team is not adjourning.
whyNot.3: Norming means agreed ways of working; this team has lost them, and ignoring conflict lets it grow.

C.q: At project closure, a team that has worked closely together for eighteen months is being disbanded. Which leader action best fits this stage?
options: Set clear roles for the next phase
C.why: At adjourning the leader recognises achievement, captures lessons learned and helps people move on.

whyNot.0: Setting roles is a forming activity, and there is no next phase for this team.
whyNot.1: Coaching through conflict is a storming activity.
whyNot.3: Closer supervision has no purpose when the work is complete.

C.q: Which TWO statements about the storming stage are correct? 1. It is a normal stage most teams pass through  2. It shows the team was badly chosen  3. The leader should help resolve conflict openly  4. The leader should suppress all disagreement
C.why: Storming is a normal stage (1), and the leader helps the team resolve conflict openly (3).

whyNot.0: Storming does not mean the team was badly chosen (2); most teams go through it.
whyNot.1: Statements 2 and 4 are both wrong: storming is normal and should be managed, not suppressed.
whyNot.3: Suppressing disagreement (4) hides the conflict; it needs to be resolved openly.

reteach.title: Think of a new house share
reteach.question: Five strangers move into a shared house for a year. How do they go from awkward strangers to a household that runs itself?

blocks.body: In the first week everyone is polite and checks with the landlord about everything (forming). A month in, rows break out over washing-up and noise (storming). Then a cleaning rota and quiet hours are agreed (norming). By spring the house runs itself and nobody needs reminding (performing). At the end of the year everyone moves out, shares a farewell meal and swaps tips for next time (adjourning).

blocks.text: If a new housemate arrives in spring, expect a few rows again: change can send a team back to storming.

explain.body: The group has just come together. Members are polite, unsure of their roles and dependent on the leader. The leader directs: sets goals, defines roles and agrees ground rules.

test.q: Why does the leader need to be directive during forming?
options: Members are unsure and rely on the leader
Members are in open conflict over roles
Members are now preparing to leave the team
test.why: In forming, members are unsure of goals and roles and depend on the leader for direction.

whyNot.1: Open conflict over roles describes storming.

explain.body: Members start to assert themselves, challenging roles, the approach and sometimes the leader. It is uncomfortable but normal. The leader coaches, manages conflict openly and clarifies roles.

test.q: Which behaviour is typical of the storming stage?
options: Polite, cautious getting to know you
test.why: Storming is when members challenge roles, the approach and each other.

explain.body: In norming the team agrees ways of working and becomes cohesive; the leader supports and facilitates. In performing the team works with high performance and autonomy; the leader delegates and focuses on monitoring and development.

test.q: In which stage is the team most able to work on its own, so the leader can delegate?
test.why: In performing the team is highly effective and autonomous, so the leader delegates.

whyNot.0: A forming team is unsure and needs direction.
whyNot.1: A storming team needs coaching through conflict.
whyNot.2: A norming team is still settling and needs support.

explain.body: The task is complete and the team disbands. The leader recognises the team's achievements, captures lessons learned and helps people move on to new roles. People may feel a sense of loss as well as pride.

test.q: Which leader action is LEAST appropriate during the adjourning stage?
options: Setting new norms for the next sprint
Capturing lessons learned from the work
Helping people move to new roles
test.why: Adjourning is about closing the team down; setting new working norms belongs to norming in an ongoing team.

whyNot.1: Recognising achievement is a key adjourning action.
whyNot.2: Capturing lessons learned is a key adjourning action.
whyNot.3: Helping people move on is a key adjourning action.
